html:
Safia Iqbal, 17, hadn’t seen her weight in months.

Diagnosed with anorexia nervosa, she and her mother knew how quickly seeing her weight would cause her to spiral.

Her mother, Hafsa Iqbal, removed the scale from their home following a therapist’s guidance, and it had helped. And that summer before her senior year, Iqbal chose to take another step in her recovery by entering an outpatient treatment facility – hoping to build a healthier relationship with food and her weight.

But from the first day of the program, staff began showing Iqbal the numbers on the scale, without her mother’s knowledge.

And on the sixth day, Iqbal learned she had gained 3.5 pounds.

She was gutted.

So, she went home and swallowed 16 pills.

attrs.caption: I don't think they provided enough safety in that kind of space where people are coming in so vulnerable
attrs.cite: Safia Iqbal, 17 years old, former patient at outpatient center

html:
Iqbal’s suicide attempt reveals the devastating stakes when eating disorder care goes wrong. Despite her well-documented medical history, The Renfrew Center — a national for-profit network that promises patient recovery using its proprietary model — missed the obvious warning signs which culminated in a teenager’s suicide attempt.

Then, to cover its tracks, employees sought to backdate Iqbal's treatment records to hide that it had not followed its own standards of care, records show.

An investigation using documents, interviews from former patients and employees, personal journals, and medical records show account after account where patients left worse off than they went in, and how Renfrew’s promises repeatedly conflict with its practices. The center markets itself as a provider of individualized, evidence-based care delivered by highly trained staff in a safe, supportive environment.

But the investigation found a different reality: a standardized treatment model that often leaves little room for individual needs, with patients describing a one-size-fits-all approach that overrode their personal treatment histories and recovery goals. Former patients said the model frequently prioritized uniformity over personalization, including requiring patients to eat the same amount of food regardless of their diagnosis, weight, or nutritional needs.

attrs.caption: They don't offer individualized care
attrs.cite: – former employee who spoke on the condition of anonymity

html: Patients and employees also described practices that, in some cases, worsened symptoms — including isolating patients from their peers, restricting autonomy, and routinely exposing them to triggers such as their weight despite known risks. Documents, interviews, and treatment records further reveal chronic understaffing and inadequate training that contributed to failures to recognize and respond to patient safety concerns, including escalating self-harm, suicidal ideation, and severe emotional distress.

attrs.caption: Journal entry excerpt from Rebecca Lebo's  journal during her stay at the Coconut Creek residential center.
Journal entry excerpts from Brenna Hallman's  journal during her stay at the Spring Lane residential center.

html:
Renfrew’s shortcomings are especially consequential because of the influence it has over the industry and the policy that governs recovery. It’s a pioneer among its peers, influencing how treatment is delivered far beyond its own centers.

Even some of its top executives hold board positions on many of the leading non-profits within the eating disorder treatment industry, while also holding an annual conference featuring celebrity speakers and offering training sessions for students and medical professionals.

Unlike traditional hospitals which are subject to state and federal regulations, eating disorder treatment facilities that do not accept Medicaid, like The Renfrew Center, are not subject to federal oversight. Instead, most treatment facilities are overseen by non-profit accreditation systems which can take the place of state regulations and are shielded from open record laws.

According to experts, the result is a mostly self-regulated industry that lacks accountability.

For patients like Rebecca Lebo, that lack of oversight left few options. Lebo entered Renfrew expecting the support the facility promised her.

Healing through community, as its website states.

Instead, after struggling to complete meals, Lebo’s access to the community was taken away as punishment rather than used as a source of support. She said staff restricted her ability to advance through the program, isolated her to a single community room for months, and placed her in a high-surveillance bedroom known as the fishbowl.

She wasn’t allowed to go outdoors for nearly three months. Lebo said the loss of autonomy worsened her depression and fed suicidal thoughts leading her to self-harm, while her repeated pleas to staff for help went unanswered.

When she considered leaving, staff threatened her with a discharge against medical advice, a designation that could jeopardize insurance coverage for any future treatment at any other facility. Because of this threat, she stayed until her insurance ran out and continued to languish within the program that had promised to help her.

attrs.caption: I was so scared. I was having panic attacks nonstop. I had to unlearn everything that I learned at Renfrew to then start my recovery journey again

html:
Renfrew promotes its model as one of the most successful for treating eating disorders, but experts told us some of its core practices - including routinely showing patients their weight - can increase anxiety, trigger relapse, and, in extreme cases, contribute to suicide attempts, as it did with Iqbal.

But some leaders at Renfrew say the harm to the patients is the patients’ fault, despite the center promising to give them the tools to emotionally regulate.

“The reason that they attempted suicide in the first place was because they didn’t have the emotional regulation skills to handle the trigger… to me, it’s got a lot to do with emotion regulation and less to do with the safety of the facility,” said Dr. Dee Ross Franklin, a previous Renfrew Center clinical training specialist who helped implement the center’s treatment model.

However, former patients describe not receiving the promised tools for recovery. Instead, they report that their emotional wellbeing was repeatedly disregarded, while the program’s exposure therapy protocols — such as “open weights” — contributed to increased self-harm. One former employee, who said she refused to show patients their weight despite protocol, argued that Renfrew’s model is overly simplistic. She called the center’s philosophy insulting because it reduces these complex diagnoses to little more than an attempt to avoid uncomfortable emotions.

Iqbal and Lebo are just two of an estimated 28 million people who struggle with an eating disorder in the United States. Eating disorders have the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric condition, with one death occurring every 52 to 54 minutes, according to the National Association of Anorexia Nervosa and Associated Disorders. Yet they remain deeply misunderstood, difficult to treat, under-researched, and often lacking consensus around what recovery should look like.

We spoke with over a dozen former patients, several former employees, researchers and advocates from across the country, each offering a different perspective on Renfrew’s system that is both widely trusted in the field and increasingly questioned.

attrs.caption: All I really experienced there was people telling me what I was doing wrong and it just adds a new level of shame

html:
What emerged was not a simple story of success or failure, but a for-profit model rigid enough to override individual needs — one that has harmed some patients even as others, and some clinicians, credit it with their recovery. And it is a model often treated as settled science, despite thin evidence and a field still early in understanding the disorders it treats.

And for patients like Iqbal and Lebo who the system failed, the cost was not just treatment that didn’t work. It was real life harm that set them both back years in their recovery journey.
